Adolescence — The Early Permanent Dentition
  • Adolescence is a sexual phenomenon, the period of life when sexual maturity is attained. More specifically, it is the transitional period between the juvenile stage and adulthood, during which secondary sexual characteristics appear, the adolescent growth spurt takes place, fertility is attained, and profound physiologic changes occur.
  • This period is particularly important in dental and orthodontic treatment because the physical changes at adolescence significantly affect the face and dentition, include:
    • Exchange from the mixed to the permanent dentition
    • Acceleration in the overall rate of facial growth
    • Differential growth of the jaws
Revised definition (7th) The 7th edition opens instead: "Adolescence is the phase of life between childhood and adulthood." It drops the 6th's "sexual phenomenon … fertility is attained" framing (above) and removes the old passage describing "feminine males and masculine females."

I Initiation of Adolescence

  • Puberty begins when pulsatile release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) from the hypothalamus increases significantly, which in turn activate release of both estrogens and androgens from the adrenal gland and ovaries or testes Fig 4.1
  • "Pituitary gonadotropins" function is to stimulate endocrine cells in both the adrenal glands and the developing sex organs to produce sex hormones in quantities sufficient to cause development of secondary sexual characteristics and accelerated growth of the genitalia.
  • The changes in the growth curves for the jaws, general body, lymphoid, and genital tissues, however, can be considered the result of the hormonal changes that accompany sexual maturation Fig 4.2
New in 7th The 7th edition reframes initiation around epigenetic control: the GnRH neurosecretory cells produce GnRH before and after puberty under epigenetic regulation, and there is emerging evidence for epigenetic roles in precocious puberty (new references). It also notes neural growth is essentially complete by age 6 to 7.

II Timing of Puberty

  • There is a great deal of individual variation, but puberty and the adolescent growth spurt occur on the average nearly 2 years earlier in girls than in boys Fig 4.3, and the timing of puberty is a highly heritable trait.
  • The stage of development of secondary sexual characteristics provides a physiologic calendar of adolescence that correlates with the individual's physical growth status.
  • Adolescence in girls can be divided into three stages: (Duration: 3½ years)
    • Stage I, occurs at about the beginning of the physical growth spurt, appearance of breast buds and early stages of the development of pubic hair.
    • Stage II, The peak velocity for physical growth "about 1 year after the initiation of stage I". At this time, there is noticeable breast development. Pubic hair is darker and more widespread, axillary hair appears.
    • Stage III, occurs 1 to 1½ years after stage II and is marked by the onset of menstruation (menarche). By this time, the growth spurt is all but complete.
  • Adolescence in boys can be divided into four stages: (Duration: 5 years)
    • Stage I, the initial sign of sexual maturation in boys usually is the "fat spurt."
    • Stage II, about 1 year after stage I, the spurt in height is just beginning, there is a redistribution and relative decrease in subcutaneous fat, pubic hair begins to appear, and growth of the penis begins.
    • Stage III, 8 to 12 months after stage II and coincides with the peak velocity in gain in height. At this time, axillary hair appears and facial hair appears on the upper lip only. A spurt in muscle growth also occurs.
    • Stage IV, occurs anywhere from 15 to 24 months after stage III, and is difficult to pinpoint. At this time, the spurt of growth in height ends, there is facial hair on the chin and the upper lip.
  • The timing of puberty makes an important difference in ultimate body size: the earlier the onset of puberty, the smaller the adult size, and vice versa. (from Fig 2.6: the earlier the adolescent growth spurt occurs, the more intense it appears to be)
Updated staging (7th) The 7th edition reclassifies puberty using Tanner's five stages for both sexes (your summary, from the 6th, gives three stages for girls and four for boys); Stage 1 is prepuberty and the final stage is adult. It also gives the end of the boys' height spurt as 17 to 20 years.
  • Growth in height depends on endochondral bone growth at the epiphyseal plates of the long bones, and the impact of the sex hormones on endochondral bone growth is twofold. Thus during the rapid growth at adolescence, the cartilage is used up faster than it is replaced. Toward the end of adolescence, the last of the cartilage is transformed into bone. At that point, growth potential is lost and growth in height stops.
  • The timing of puberty seems to be affected by both genetic and environmental influences:
    • In girls, the onset of menstruation requires the development of a certain amount of body fat.
    • Athletic girls with low body fat often are slow to begin their menstrual periods.
  • Seasonal and cultural factors also can affect the overall rate of physical growth:
    • Growth tends to be faster in spring and summer than in fall and winter
    • City children tend to mature faster than rural ones.
  • Growth of the jaws usually correlates with the physiologic events of puberty in about the same way as growth in height Fig 4.5
  • There is an adolescent growth spurt in the length of the mandible, though not nearly as dramatic a spurt as that in body height, and a modest although discernible increase in growth at the sutures of the maxilla. "follow the cephalocaudal gradient of growth"
  • Although jaw growth follows the curve for general body growth, the correlation is not perfect. A significant number of individuals, especially among girls, have a "juvenile acceleration" in jaw growth (can equal or even exceed the jaw growth that accompanies secondary sexual maturation) that occurs 1 to 2 years before the adolescent growth spurt Fig 4.6. In boys, if a juvenile spurt occurs, it is nearly always less intense than the growth acceleration at puberty.
  • In early-maturing girls, the adolescent growth spurt often precedes the final transition of the dentition. If they are to receive orthodontic treatment while they are growing rapidly, treatment must begin during the mixed dentition rather than after all succedaneous teeth eruption.
Growth Patterns in the Dentofacial Complex

I Dimensional Changes

Growth of the Nasomaxillary Complex

  • Growth of the nasomaxillary area is produced by two basic mechanisms:
    1. Passive displacement, growth in the cranial base pushes maxilla forward. Fig 4.7
    2. Active growth of the maxillary structures and nose. Fig 4.8
  • Cranial base synchondroses close at about age 7, most of the growth after that time is due to active growth at the maxillary sutures and surfaces.
  • The maxilla grows downward and forward as bone is added in the tuberosity area posteriorly and at the posterior and superior sutures, but the anterior surfaces of the bone are resorbing at the same time.
  • Nose grows more rapidly than the rest of the face, particularly during the adolescent growth spurt "by an increase in size of the cartilaginous nasal septum, and proliferation of the lateral cartilages".
  • On average, nasal dimensions increase at a rate about 25% greater than growth of the maxilla during adolescence (but growth of the nose is extremely variable)
  • The more prominent the nose, the more prominent the jaws need to be to produce reasonable facial balance.

Mandibular Growth

  • On the average, ramus height increases 1 to 2 mm per year and body length increases 2 to 3 mm per year.
  • The increase in chin prominence with maturity results from a combination of forward translation of the chin as a part of the overall growth of the mandible and resorption above the chin (area between chin and alveolar bone) that alters the bony contours.
  • An important source of variability in how much the chin grows forward is the extent of growth changes at the glenoid fossa. Usually, the attachment point moves straight down, so that there is no anteroposterior displacement of the mandible, but occasionally it moves posteriorly, thus subtracting from rather than augmenting the forward projection of the chin. Fig 4.10

Timing of Growth in Width, Length, and Height

  • Growth in width is completed first, then growth in length, finally growth in height.
  • The width of the dental arches, tends to be completed before the adolescent growth spurt and is affected minimally if at all by adolescent growth changes. For instance, intercanine width is more likely to decrease than increase after age 12.
  • Growth in length and height of both jaws continues through the period of puberty.
  • In both sexes, growth in vertical height of the face continues longer than growth in length, with the late vertical growth occurring primarily in the mandible.
  • Increases in facial height and concomitant eruption of teeth continue throughout life, but the decline to the adult level often does not occur until the early 20s in boys and somewhat earlier in girls.
New in 7th The 7th edition adds sex differences in late growth: forward growth of the mandible is greater in males than in females, and the late vertical growth occurs primarily in the maxilla in females but more in the mandible in males.

II Rotation of Jaws During Growth

Implant Studies of Jaw Rotation (Björk and coworkers in Copenhagen)

  • Terminology: Table 4.2
    • The Core of the Mandible: The bone that surrounds the inferior alveolar nerve.
    • Mandibular Functional Processes: Alveolar process (bone supporting the teeth and providing for mastication), the muscular processes (the bone to which the muscles of mastication attach), and the condylar process. Fig 4.13
    • Internal Rotation: Rotation of mandibular core relative to cranial base (not visible)
    • External Rotation: Rotation of mandibular plane relative to core of mandible "surface changes".
    • Total Rotation: Rotation of mandibular plane (or palatal plane in maxilla) relative to cranial base. (visible)
  • If implants are placed in areas of stable bone away from the functional processes, it can be observed that in most individuals, the core of the mandible rotates (internal rotation) during growth in a way that would tend to decrease the mandibular plane angle (i.e., up anteriorly and down posteriorly) Fig 4.14. either by rotation around the condyle (Matrix rotation) or rotation centered within the body of the mandible (Intramatrix rotation).
  • The rotation of either jaw is considered "forward" and given a negative sign if there is more growth posteriorly than anteriorly (chin upward and forward). The rotation is "backward" and given a positive direction if it lengthens anterior dimensions more than posterior ones (chin downward and backward).
  • Mandible:
    • Internal rotation of the mandible ranging up to 10 to 15 degrees "forward" Fig 4.15. Of this, about 25% results from rotation at the condyle (Matrix) and 75% results from rotation within the body of the mandible (Intramatrix).
    • When the core of the mandible rotates forward an average of 15 degrees, the mandibular plane angle rotates only 2 to 4 degrees "forward" on average. "because surface changes (external rotation) tend to compensate".
    • This means that the posterior part of the lower border of the mandible must be an area of resorption, whereas the anterior aspect of the lower border is unchanged or undergoes slight apposition.
  • Maxilla:
    • If implants are placed above the maxillary alveolar process, however, one can observe a core of the maxilla undergoes a small and variable degree of rotation "internal rotation", forward or backward Fig 4.17.
    • At the same time there also external rotation "varying degrees of modeling of the palate and in the amount of eruption of the incisors and molars"
    • For most patients, the external rotation is opposite in direction and equal in magnitude to the internal rotation, so that the two rotations cancel and the net change in jaw orientation (as evaluated by the palatal plane) is zero (or usually rotates few degrees forward, but backward rotation occurs frequently)
  • The rotational patterns of growth are quite different for individuals who have short-face and long-face types of vertical facial development.
  • Short-face Type: Fig 4.22Fig 4.23
    • Have excessive forward rotation of the mandible during growth, resulting from both an increase in the normal internal rotation and a decrease in external compensation.
    • The result is a nearly horizontal palatal plane, a low mandibular plane angle, and a large gonial angle.
    • A deep bite malocclusion and crowded incisors (lower?) usually accompany this type of rotation.
Corrected in 7th For the short-face type the 7th edition gives a nearly horizontal palatal plane, a low mandibular-plane angle, and a smaller gonial angle — a correction of the "large gonial angle" above, and consistent with the low mandibular-plane angle.
  • Long-face Type: Fig 4.19
    • Result primarily from a lack of the normal forward internal rotation of the mandible or even a backward internal rotation.
    • The internal rotation, in turn, is primarily centered at the condyle. (remember 25% of total internal rotation)
    • The result is excessive lower anterior face height, the palatal plane rotates down posteriorly, often creating a negative rather than the normal positive inclination to the true horizontal. The mandible shows an opposite, backward rotation, with an increase in the mandibular plane angle.
    • Associated with anterior open bite malocclusion and mandibular deficiency (because the chin rotates back as well as down).
    • Backward rotation of the mandible also occurs in patients with abnormalities or pathologic changes affecting the TMJs whom growth at the condyle is restricted.

Interaction Between Jaw Rotation and Tooth Eruption

  • The rotational pattern of jaw growth obviously influences the magnitude of tooth eruption and the direction of eruption and the ultimate anteroposterior position of the incisor teeth.
  • Maxilla:
    • The path of eruption of the maxillary teeth is downward and somewhat forward Fig 4.17.
    • In normal growth, the maxilla usually rotates a few degrees forward but frequently rotates slightly backward. Forward rotation would tend to tip the incisors forward, increasing their prominence, whereas backward rotation directs the anterior teeth more posteriorly, relatively uprighting them.
    • Movement of the teeth relative to the cranial base obviously could be produced by a combination of translocation as the tooth moved along with the jaw (contributes about half the total maxillary tooth movement), and true eruption, movement of the tooth within its jaw Fig 4.20.
  • Mandible:
    • The eruption path of mandibular teeth is upward and somewhat forward.
    • The normal internal rotation of the mandible carries the jaw upward in front. This rotation alters the eruption path of the incisors, tending to direct them more posteriorly Fig 4.21.
    • Because the internal jaw rotation tends to upright the incisors, the molars migrate further mesially during growth than do the incisors, and this migration is reflected in the decrease in arch length that normally occurs.
    • Because the forward internal rotation of the mandible is greater than that of the maxilla, it is not surprising that the normal decrease in mandibular arch length is somewhat greater than the decrease in maxillary arch length "changes in anteroposterior position of the incisor teeth are a major influence on arch length changes"
  • When excessive rotation occurs in the short-face type of development, the incisors tend to be carried into an overlapping position. This is why there is a strong tendency for deep bite malocclusion in short-face type.
  • In the long-face growth pattern, on the other hand, an anterior open bite will develop as anterior face height increases unless the incisors erupt for an extreme distance. The rotation of the jaws also carries the incisors forward, creating dental protrusion (not necessarily, lip pressure?)
Maturational and Aging Changes

I Facial Growth in Adult

  • According to Behrens's study, facial growth had continued during adult life "continues to show a cephalocaudal gradient (i.e., more mandibular than maxillary changes in adult life)"
  • There is an increase in essentially all the facial dimensions. Vertical changes in adult life were more prominent than anteroposterior changes, whereas width changes were least evident.
  • It appears that a woman's first pregnancy often produces some growth of her jaws.
  • Although the magnitude of the adult growth changes was quite small, the cumulative effect over decades was surprisingly large Fig 4.25.
  • Rotation of both jaws continued into adult life. In general, males showed a net rotation of the jaws in a forward direction, slightly decreasing the mandibular plane angle, whereas females had a tendency toward backward rotation, with an increase in the mandibular plane angle.
  • Changes in the facial soft tissue profile were greater than changes in the facial skeleton "involve an elongation of the nose (which often became significantly longer during adult life), flattening of the lips, and an augmentation of the soft tissue chin".
  • In summary: Width "transverse" changes are quite low. Anteroposterior growth continues at a noticeable rate for a longer period, declining to basal levels only after puberty, with small but noticeable changes continuing throughout adult life. Vertical growth, continues well after puberty in both males and females, also continues at a modest level far into adult life.
New in 7th The 7th edition summarizes adult landmark movement by sex: female skeletal landmarks moved downward and posteriorly, while male landmarks moved more downward and anteriorly.

II Changes in Facial Soft Tissues

  • The change of greatest significance for orthodontists is that the lips, and the other soft tissues of the face, sag downward with aging. The result is a decrease in exposure of the upper incisors and an increase in exposure of the lower incisors, both at rest and on smile Figs 4.27. The lips also become progressively thinner, with less vermilion display Fig 4.29.
  • It is important to remember in orthodontic treatment that the vertical relationship of the lip to the teeth will change after adolescence. leaving the upper incisors somewhat more exposed than the ideal adult relationship is necessary in treatment of an adolescent, if this relationship is to be ideal later in life Fig 4.30.
New in 7th New soft-tissue data: in males the peak in nasal growth is ~13–14 years, continuing to 16–18 years and beyond; soft-tissue thickness at pogonion averages 2.4 mm in males and 1.5 mm in females; and chin prominence can also result from posterior placement of the mandibular incisors. With age the philtrum lengthens, peaking in the mid-20s for both sexes.

III Changes in Alignment and Occlusion

  • In modern populations, there is a strong tendency for crowding of the mandibular incisors to develop in the late teens and early 20s, no matter how well aligned the teeth were initially. These changes appear as early as age 17 to 18 in some individuals and as late as the mid-20s in others.
  • Three major theories to account for this crowding have been proposed:
    1. Lack of "normal attrition" in the modern diet. With a coarse diet, the width of teeth is reduced as interproximal wear occur. The result in many primitive populations was a reduction in arch circumference of 10 mm or more after completion of the permanent dentition at adolescence. Raymond Begg, concluded that in modern populations the teeth became crowded when attrition did not occur with soft diets, and advocated widespread extraction of premolar teeth to provide the equivalent of the attrition he saw in aborigines. But, it has been observed in other population groups that late crowding may develop even after premolars have been extracted. Thus the Begg theory, although superficially attractive, does not explain late crowding.
    2. Pressure from third molars. In fact, late crowding of lower incisors can and often does develop in individuals whose lower third molars are congenitally missing. There is some evidence that incisor crowding may be lessened by early removal of second molars, which presumably would relieve pressure from third molars, but pressure from third molars clearly is not the total explanation either.
    3. Late Mandibular Growth. Because of the cephalocaudal gradient of growth, the mandible can and does grow more in the late teens than the maxilla. The position of the dentition relative to the maxilla and mandible is influenced by the pattern of growth of the jaws. When the mandible grows forward relative to the maxilla, as it usually does in the late teens, the mandibular incisor teeth tend to be displaced lingually, particularly if forward rotation is also present. One of three things must happen:
      • A. The mandible is displaced distally, accompanied by a distortion of TMJ function and displacement of the articular disc. (Rare) Fig 4.10.B
      • B. The upper incisors are forward, opening space between these teeth (Rare)
      • C. The lower incisors displace distally and become crowded. (Usual response)
  • It is not even necessary for incisors to be in occlusal contact for late crowding to develop. This also occurs commonly in individuals who have an anterior open bite and backward, not forward, rotation of the mandible "the rotation of the mandible carries the dentition forward, thrusting the incisors against the lip" Fig 4.19
  • The current concept is that late incisor crowding almost always develops as the mandibular incisors move distally relative to the body of the mandible late in mandibular growth, and lower third molars could be the "last straw" in a chain of events that led to late incisor crowding.
New in 7th Within the Begg / third-molar discussion the 7th edition adds management of the leeway space to accommodate the transitional crowding alongside early removal of second molars as ways to relieve pressure from third molars.

IV Aging Changes in Teeth and Supporting Structure

  • As time passes, additional dentin slowly deposits on the inside of the tooth so that the pulp chamber gradually becomes smaller with increasing age. This process continues relatively rapidly until the late teens, at which time the pulp chamber of a typical permanent tooth is about half the size that it was at the time of initial eruption. Additional dentin continues to be produced at a slower rate throughout life.
  • Apical movement of the gingival attachment (in normal circumstances) results more from vertical growth of the jaws and the accompanying eruption of the teeth than from downward migration of the gingival attachment.
  • In the late teens, the gingival attachment is usually near the cementoenamel junction. In the absence of inflammation, mechanical abrasion or pathologic changes, the gingival attachment should remain at about the same level almost indefinitely.
  • At one time, it was thought that "passive eruption" (defined as an actual gingival migration of the attachment without any eruption of the tooth) occurred. It now appears that as long as the gingival tissues are entirely healthy, this sort of downward migration of the soft tissue attachment does not occur. What was once thought to be apical migration of the gingiva during the teens is really "active eruption", compensating for the vertical jaw growth still occurring at that time. Fig 4.35
